pages.title: 3D Graphing Calculator: Plot z = f(x, y) Surfaces Online | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free 3D graphing calculator and surface plotter. Type z = f(x, y), rotate and zoom the surface, set ranges, use sliders and save a PNG.
intro: This 3D graphing calculator plots a surface z = f(x, y). Type a formula in x and y, then drag to rotate the surface, scroll or pinch to zoom, and use the range boxes to choose which part of the surface to see. Letters other than x and y, such as a or b, become sliders so you can watch how a parameter changes the shape. It also draws implicit surfaces such as the sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9 when you type an equation that contains z.

ul: Type the right-hand side only, for example x^2 + y^2. Starting with z = is also fine.
For a closed or implicit surface, type an equation in x, y and z, such as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9. The plotter finds every point where both sides are equal.
Use * for multiplication or write sin(x)cos(y). Use ^ for powers and sqrt(), abs() or |x| for roots and absolute value.
Functions include sin, cos, tan, exp, ln, log, sqrt and abs. Angles are in radians.
Any other single letter, such as a or b, becomes a slider from −5 to 5.
Drag (or use the arrow keys) to rotate, scroll or pinch to zoom, and double-click to reset the view.
Top view looks straight down on the surface with no perspective, so the colours read like a contour map of height.
Detail sets the grid resolution. Use Fine for smooth curves and Fast on slower phones. Implicit surfaces use a 3D grid, so Fast is a good choice for the busiest ones.
For an implicit surface, z min and z max set the height of the box (default −6 to 6). Widen the ranges if part of the surface is cut off.
Set z min and z max to clip tall spikes so you can see the interesting part of surfaces such as 1/(x^2 + y^2).
Paraboloid: z = x^2 + y^2, a bowl that opens upward.
Saddle: z = x^2 − y^2, which curves up along one axis and down along the other.
Ripple: z = sin(sqrt(x^2 + y^2)), circular waves around the origin.
Gaussian: z = exp(−(x^2 + y^2)/4), a smooth hill.
Cone: z = sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
Monkey saddle: z = x^3 − 3xy^2, which has room for three downward slopes.
Sphere: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9.
Torus: (sqrt(x^2 + y^2) − 3)^2 + z^2 = 1, a doughnut.
Hyperboloid: x^2 + y^2 − z^2 = 1, an hourglass that opens up and down.
Gyroid: sin(x)cos(y) + sin(y)cos(z) + sin(z)cos(x) = 0, a repeating sponge-like sheet.

p: The colour shows height: dark purple is the lowest point in view and yellow is the highest, and the colour bar at the right lists the values. The numbers on the box edges show the x and y ranges. Because the height axis is scaled to fit the box, compare heights using the numbers rather than the visual size alone.

faq.q: Can it plot a sphere or other implicit surfaces such as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9?
faq.a: Yes. Type the equation with z on either side, for example x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9. The plotter samples the box and extracts the surface with a method called marching tetrahedra. Inequalities such as x^2 + y^2 + z^2 < 9 are not supported.

faq.q: Why are parts of my surface missing?
faq.a: Points where the formula has no real value, such as the square root of a negative number or division by zero, are left blank. Points outside your z min and z max limits are also left blank.

faq.q: Why is my surface a flat sheet or very spiky?
faq.a: A very tall spike makes the rest of the surface look flat because the height is scaled to fit. Set z min and z max, or narrow the x and y ranges, to zoom into the part you care about.

faq.q: Does it work on a phone?
faq.a: Yes. Drag with one finger to rotate and pinch with two fingers to zoom. If the surface is slow to draw, choose Fast detail.

faq.q: Are angles in degrees or radians?
faq.a: Radians, so sin(x) uses x in radians, as in most calculus courses.

faq.q: Can I save the picture?
faq.a: Use Save PNG to download the current view as an image.

pages.title: Z-Score Calculator: Find z, Percentile & Probability | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free z-score calculator. Convert a value to a z-score, find a value from z or a percentile, and get normal-curve probabilities with a shaded bell curve.
intro: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean. Positive means above the mean, negative means below, and zero means exactly average. This calculator converts a raw value to a z-score, turns a z-score or percentile back into a value, and finds the probability (area under the normal curve) for one tail, a middle range or both tails.
It assumes the data is roughly normal, which is the usual setting for z-score and percentile questions in AP Statistics and introductory college statistics.

p: z = (x − μ) / σ, where x is the value, μ is the mean and σ is the standard deviation. To go back from a z-score to a value, use x = μ + zσ. If you only have a sample, the same formula works with the sample mean and sample standard deviation.

A test has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 10. A score of 85 gives z = (85 − 70) / 10 = 1.5. The area to the left of z = 1.5 is about 0.9332, so the score is at about the 93rd percentile and roughly 6.7% of scores are higher. The calculator opens with these numbers already filled in.

ul: Left tail, P(X < a): the share of values below a. This is the percentile.
Right tail, P(X > a): the share of values above a.
Between a and b: the probability that a value falls inside the range.
Outside a and b: the probability in both tails together, which is what two-sided tests use.

p: In a normal distribution about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean (z between −1 and 1), about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. That is why values beyond z = ±2 are called unusual and beyond ±3 are rare.

ul: z = 1.645 is the 95th percentile (a 5% right tail).
z = 1.96 is the 97.5th percentile and marks the middle 95%.
z = 2.576 is the 99.5th percentile and marks the middle 99%.

faq.q: What is a good z-score?
faq.a: It depends on what you are measuring. A z-score only says how far a value is from the mean. For test scores a high positive z means a high percentile, while for something like error rates a low or negative z is better. In a normal distribution, values beyond ±2 are unusual and beyond ±3 are rare.

faq.q: Can a z-score be negative?
faq.a: Yes. A negative z-score means the value is below the mean. A z-score of −1.2 is 1.2 standard deviations below average.

faq.q: How do I find a z-score from a percentile?
faq.a: Choose “Z-score and value from a percentile”, then enter the percentile. For example, the 90th percentile is z ≈ 1.2816.

faq.q: What is the difference between a z-score and a t-score?
faq.a: A z-score uses the normal distribution, normally with a known or assumed standard deviation. A t statistic uses the sample standard deviation and the t distribution, which has heavier tails when the sample is small. For tests on means from small samples, use the t-test calculator.

faq.q: Does it work if my data is not normal?
faq.a: You can always compute a z-score, but the probabilities and percentiles assume a normal distribution. For skewed data they can be misleading, so check a histogram first.

faq.q: Is a z-score the same as a standard score?
faq.a: Yes. Standard score and z-score mean the same thing: the number of standard deviations a value is from the mean.

pages.title: Standard Deviation Calculator (Sample & Population) with Steps | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free standard deviation calculator. Paste your data for sample and population SD, variance, mean, standard error and a step-by-step table.
intro: Standard deviation measures how spread out numbers are around their mean. A small value means the data sits close to the average, and a large value means it is more spread out. Paste your numbers and this calculator returns the sample and population versions, plus variance, mean, median, range, standard error and a step-by-step table of deviations.

p: Use population standard deviation (divide by n) when your numbers are the whole group you care about, such as every score in a class of 25. Use sample standard deviation (divide by n − 1) when your numbers are a sample from a larger group and you want to estimate that group's spread. Dividing by n − 1 is called Bessel's correction. Most statistics courses expect the sample formula unless the problem says the data is a population.

ul: Mean: x̄ = Σx / n
Sample variance: s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)
Population variance: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N
Standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
Standard error of the mean: s / √n

p: For 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 7, 9, 5 the mean is 47 / 8 = 5.875 and the sum of squared deviations is 28.875. The sample variance is 28.875 / 7 = 4.125, so the sample standard deviation is about 2.031. The population variance is 28.875 / 8 = 3.609, so the population standard deviation is about 1.900. The calculator opens with this data.

sections.h: What a standard deviation tells you
p: Standard deviation is in the same units as your data, unlike variance, which is in squared units. In a roughly normal data set about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. Because every value is squared in the calculation, outliers have a large effect, so check for extreme values.

faq.q: What is the difference between variance and standard deviation?
faq.a: Variance is the average squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation is its square root, which puts the spread back into the original units of the data.

faq.q: Can standard deviation be negative?
faq.a: No. It is a square root, so it is zero or positive. It is zero only when every value in the data set is identical.

faq.q: How many numbers do I need?
faq.a: At least 2 for a sample standard deviation, because the formula divides by n − 1. Larger samples give more reliable estimates.

faq.q: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
faq.a: Standard deviation describes how spread out individual values are. Standard error of the mean (s divided by the square root of n) describes how much the sample mean would vary from sample to sample.

faq.q: How do outliers affect the result?
faq.a: A single extreme value can increase the standard deviation a lot. If your data has outliers, also look at the median and the range, or use a measure such as the interquartile range.

faq.q: Can I paste data from a spreadsheet?
faq.a: Yes. Copy a column from Excel or Google Sheets and paste it in. Numbers can be separated by commas, spaces or new lines, and negative numbers and decimals work.

pages.title: Confidence Interval Calculator for a Mean or Proportion | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free confidence interval calculator for a mean (t or z) or a proportion (Wilson and Wald). See margin of error, critical value and a shaded graph.
intro: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on a sample. This calculator builds an interval for a population mean from a sample mean, standard deviation and sample size, or for a proportion from a count of successes. Choose 90%, 95%, 99% or your own confidence level.

ul: Mean, σ unknown: x̄ ± t* · s/√n, with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Mean, σ known: x̄ ± z* · σ/√n
Proportion, Wald: p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n)
Proportion, Wilson: re-centres and adjusts the width, and works better for small samples or proportions near 0 or 1.

p: A sample of n = 36 has a mean of 52.4 and a standard deviation of 6.8. The standard error is 6.8 / 6 = 1.133. For 95% confidence with 35 degrees of freedom, t* is about 2.030, so the margin of error is about 2.30 and the interval is about (50.10, 54.70). The calculator opens with these numbers.

Use t when the population standard deviation is unknown, which is almost always the case with real data. Use z only when the population standard deviation is known from outside your sample. With large samples the two give nearly the same answer.

sections.h: How to read a confidence interval
p: A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% chance the true value lies inside this one interval. It means that if you repeated the sampling many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value.

ul: 90% confidence: z* = 1.645
95% confidence: z* = 1.960
99% confidence: z* = 2.576

faq.q: What is the margin of error?
faq.a: It is the critical value times the standard error, which is the distance from the sample estimate to each end of the interval.

faq.q: How can I get a narrower interval?
faq.a: Use a larger sample or a lower confidence level. Quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the margin of error.

faq.q: Is a 99% interval better than a 95% interval?
faq.a: It is more likely to contain the true value, but it is wider and so less precise. The right level depends on how costly a miss would be.

faq.q: Which proportion interval should I use?
faq.a: Many textbooks teach the Wald (normal approximation) interval, so it is shown for checking homework. The Wilson interval is generally more reliable, especially when n is small or the proportion is near 0 or 1.

faq.q: What conditions do I need?
faq.a: The sample should be random and the observations independent. For a mean, the data should be roughly normal or the sample reasonably large. For a proportion, a common rule of thumb is at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

faq.q: What if I only have raw data?
faq.a: Paste your numbers into the standard deviation calculator to get the mean, standard deviation and n, then enter them here.

pages.title: T-Test Calculator: One-Sample, Two-Sample & Paired | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free t-test calculator. Run a one-sample, Welch, pooled or paired t-test from raw data or summary statistics and get t, df, p-value and a graph.
intro: A t-test checks whether a sample mean differs from a value, or whether two means differ, when the population standard deviation is unknown. Choose the test type, enter raw data or summary statistics, and the calculator returns the t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, a confidence interval and an effect size, with a shaded graph of the p-value.

ul: One-sample: compare one sample mean to a known or claimed value.
Two-sample (Welch): compare the means of two independent groups without assuming equal variances. This is the safer default.
Two-sample (pooled): the same comparison, but it assumes both groups have the same variance, and uses n₁ + n₂ − 2 degrees of freedom.
Paired: compare two measurements on the same subjects, such as before and after. The test runs on the differences.
One-sample: t = (x̄ − μ₀) / (s/√n), with n − 1 degrees of freedom
Welch: t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), with Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
Paired: t = d̄ / (sᵈ/√n), where d is each pair's difference

p: Sample 1 is 23, 25, 28, 30, 26, 27, 24, 29 (mean 26.5) and sample 2 is 20, 22, 25, 24, 21, 23, 26, 22 (mean 22.875). A Welch two-sample test gives t ≈ 3.22 with about 13.5 degrees of freedom and a two-sided p-value of about 0.0064. At α = 0.05 that is enough to reject the null hypothesis that the means are equal. The calculator opens with this data.

The p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a t statistic at least as extreme as yours. A p-value below your significance level α is evidence against the null hypothesis. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a non-significant result does not prove the means are equal.

ul: Observations are independent (or properly paired).
The data is roughly normal, or the samples are reasonably large.
There are no extreme outliers. Plot your data if you are unsure.

faq.q: Should I use Welch or the pooled t-test?
faq.a: Welch is the safer choice because it does not assume equal variances and loses little power when the variances are equal. Use the pooled test when your course or problem tells you to assume equal variances.

faq.q: When do I use a one-tailed test?
faq.a: Only when your hypothesis names a direction before you look at the data, such as “the new method scores higher”. Otherwise use the two-sided test.

faq.q: What are degrees of freedom?
faq.a: They describe how much independent information the standard deviation estimate rests on. For a one-sample or paired test it is n − 1. The Welch test uses a fractional value.

faq.q: What does Cohen's d mean?
faq.a: It is an effect size: the difference between means in standard deviation units. As a rough guide, 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large, but what counts as large depends on the field.

faq.q: Can I use a t-test on a small sample?
faq.a: Yes, if the data is roughly normal. With very small samples the test is sensitive to outliers and skew.

faq.q: Why does the paired test need two lists of the same length?
faq.a: Each value in the first list is matched with the value in the same position in the second list, and the test runs on those differences.

pages.title: Chi-Square Calculator: Goodness of Fit & Independence Test | ExamGrapher
pages.desc: Free chi-square calculator. Run a goodness-of-fit or independence test, get χ², degrees of freedom, p-value, expected counts and a shaded graph.
intro: A chi-square test compares counts. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether observed counts match an expected distribution, such as whether a die is fair. The test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are related, using a table of counts. Enter your counts and the calculator returns the chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, expected counts, each cell's contribution and a shaded graph of the p-value.

sections.h: Which chi-square test do I need?
ul: Goodness of fit: one categorical variable, compared with an expected distribution. Degrees of freedom = categories − 1.
Test of independence: two categorical variables in a contingency table. Degrees of freedom = (rows − 1) × (columns − 1).
Chi-square statistic: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E, where O is the observed count and E is the expected count
Independence, expected count: E = (row total × column total) / grand total
Cramér’s V (effect size for a table): √(χ² / (n × min(rows − 1, columns − 1)))

sections.h: Worked example: is a die fair?
p: A die is rolled 60 times and the six faces come up 5, 8, 9, 8, 10 and 20 times. If the die is fair, each face is expected 10 times. The contributions (O − E)² / E are 2.5, 0.4, 0.1, 0.4, 0 and 10, so χ² = 13.4 with 5 degrees of freedom and a p-value of about 0.0199. At α = 0.05 you reject the idea that the die is fair. The calculator opens with these counts.

sections.h: Worked example: independence in a 2 × 2 table
p: Switch to the test of independence and use the table 30, 20 / 20, 30. Every expected count is 25, so χ² = 4 × (5² / 25) = 4 with 1 degree of freedom, giving p ≈ 0.0455.

ul: Use counts, not percentages or averages.
Observations are independent and come from a random sample.
Each expected count should be at least 5. The calculator warns you when it is not.

faq.q: What does the p-value tell me?
faq.a: It is the probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of getting a chi-square statistic at least as large as yours. A p-value below your significance level is evidence against the null hypothesis. It does not tell you how strong or important the effect is.

faq.q: Can the chi-square statistic be negative?
faq.a: No. Every term (O − E)² / E is zero or positive, so the statistic is zero or positive. Large values mean the observed counts are far from the expected ones.

faq.q: What if some expected counts are below 5?
faq.a: The chi-square approximation becomes less reliable. Combine categories where that makes sense, collect more data, or use an exact test such as Fisher's exact test for a 2 × 2 table.

faq.q: Does it use the Yates continuity correction?
faq.a: No. It uses the standard formula taught in most courses. Some software applies a continuity correction to 2 × 2 tables by default, which gives a slightly different p-value.

faq.q: Can I enter percentages?
faq.a: For the independence test, enter counts. For goodness of fit, enter observed counts, and you can give the expected distribution as proportions or percentages in the custom proportions option.

faq.q: What does Cramér's V mean?
faq.a: It measures how strongly two variables are associated in a table, from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association). It helps because a large sample can make a tiny effect statistically significant.

faq.a: On paper-based tests, in classes that do not allow devices, and on exams where your own approved calculator is required. Check each test's calculator policy.

faq.q: Does ExamGrapher match TI-84 regression results?
faq.a: Yes. Linear, quadratic, cubic, exponential, power and logarithmic fits use the same least-squares methods as LinReg, QuadReg, CubicReg, ExpReg, PwrReg and LnReg.

cheatsheet.title: 2026 Test-Day Graphing Calculator Cheat Sheet | ExamGrapher
cheatsheet.desc: The graphing moves that save the most time on the Digital SAT, digital PSAT, ACT, AP Precalculus and state tests. Print it or keep it open while you practice.

items: Type both equations exactly as given, including standard form like 2x + 3y = 12. The intersection point is the solution.
No intersection means no solution (parallel lines). The same line twice means infinitely many solutions.
Type the quadratic and read the vertex (min or max) and roots from Key points.
For questions with exactly one solution, use a slider (k*x^2 + 4x + 1) and drag until the curve just touches the x-axis.
Type y > 2x + 1 to shade. A dashed boundary means strict (< or >) and a solid one means ≤ or ≥.
Plot the answer choice as a point, for example (2, 7), to see whether it falls in the shaded region.
Turn a table into points: (1, 5), (3, 9), (5, 13). Then test each answer choice's equation.
For a line of best fit, use a regression: linear for a steady trend, exponential for percentage change, quadratic for rise-and-fall data.
Check DEG and RAD before every trig question.
To solve sin(x) = 0.5, graph y = sin(x) and y = 0.5 and read the intersections.
Zoom out first, then zoom in on the point you need.
Practice with US Exam Mode on, so you can find key points without the labels.
